 Best Project Finalist and Best Project Healthcare: The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center University Hospital
 Photo courtesy Infinite Impact 
 November 9, 2026 
 The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center University Hospital 
 Columbus, Ohio
 PROJECT OF THE YEAR FINALIST and BEST PROJECT, HEALTH CARE 
 Submitted by: Walsh/Turner Joint Venture 
 Owner: The Ohio State University 
 Lead Design Firm: HDR 
 General Contractor: Walsh/Turner Joint Venture 
 Civil & Structural Engineer: MKA and EM&T 
 MEP Engineer: BR+A 
 The construction team behind Ohio State University’s 26-story University Hospital had to devise a way for the hospital to continue serving patients while construction continued.
 The 1.9-million-sq-ft medical facility is designed to significantly expand patient care and clinical capabilities on the medical campus in Columbus. It includes 820 private patient rooms, 234 intensive care beds, advanced operating and diagnostic spaces, a new emergency department and expanded maternity and neonatal care.
 “One of the project’s greatest challenges was developing a turnover strategy for a nearly 2-million-sq-ft hospital that could not simply be completed and handed over all at once,” says Jim Vinson, project executive for Walsh Construction.
 Photo courtesy Lauren K Davis / Feinknopf 
 Ohio State needed early access to completed sections for equipment installation, owner fit-out, staff training and other transition activities. Planning for some individual turnovers started as much as four years in advance, Vinson says. The process required detailed coordination of life-safety systems, inspections, access and egress and the separation of occupied areas from construction zones.
 The construction team embedded a staff member with Ohio State’s transition team, giving the owner a direct connection to someone familiar with both the building and the construction turnover process.
 “This long-range, collaborative approach allowed OSU’s transition activities to progress alongside construction rather than waiting for completion of the entire facility,” Vinson says.
 Construction began during the COVID-19 pandemic, adding labor availability, material escalation and supply-chain uncertainty to the hurdle presented by the project's size and complexity. The team responded with flexible staffing, design-assist collaboration and early procurement.
 Photo courtesy Lauren K Davis / Feinknopf 
 In some cases, raw materials were purchased in bulk well before they were needed, allowing the team to lock in pricing and secure critical supplies amid market volatility, Vinson says.
 The scope also evolved during construction. Areas originally intended to remain as shell space were advanced for full build-out, adding substantial work while construction was already underway.
 Vinson says early involvement by design-assist trade partners helped the team evaluate impacts and integrate the additional work into existing schedules and workflows.
 Approximately $200 million worth of prefabrication was incorporated into the hospital, including bathroom pods, mechanical systems, curtain wall units and mechanical, electrical and plumbing assemblies. Multitrade racks, wall assemblies and other room components allowed work that traditionally would have taken place inside the building to be performed in controlled environments. “Prefabrication was essential to delivering a project of this scale safely, efficiently and consistently,” Vinson says.
 Comprehensive 4D modeling and production tracking enabled the team to visualize construction sequences, coordinate trades and monitor progress across the sprawling project. “Prefabrication and digital planning helped transform a complex construction program into repeatable, manageable production,” Vinson says.
